---
name: cc
description: "Drive the running Cockpit server through the `cockpit` CLI — open and control browser bubbles, observe terminals, query the codegraph."
---

Enter Cockpit CLI operation mode.

The Cockpit CLI is a thin local client over the running Cockpit server: each invocation forwards to the server and reuses its CodeIndex / caches / git views.

CLI entry point selection (**default = prod**):

- Default: **`cockpit`** (prod, port 3457) — use this when no explicit dev signal is given.
- Switch to `cockpit-dev` (dev, port 3456) ONLY when the user explicitly signals dev mode, via one of:
  1. They write `cockpit-dev ...` directly in the task text.
  2. The first word after `/cc` is `dev` (e.g. `/cc dev terminal bmfb check the errors`).

Examples below use `cockpit`; only swap in `cockpit-dev` when one of the two dev signals above is present.

## Subcommands

| Subcommand | Purpose |
|---|---|
| (none) / `<path>` | Start server, open project |
| `browser open <url\|path>` | Web page → a Chrome tab; local HTML/file → a console bubble. Prints its id |
| `browser tabs` | Every open Chrome tab with its id |
| `browser <id> <action>` | Drive a tab or bubble |
| `terminal <id> [<action>]` | Read-only observation of a terminal ring buffer |
| `codegraph <subcmd>` | Project code graph (search/symbols/callers/callees/impact/file/coedit/related/affected) |
| `update` | Upgrade to latest npm version |

## Typical usage pattern

Terminal / browser bubbles in the UI carry a 4-char short id (e.g. `bmfb` / `mpcw`). After `/cc` users typically follow with `cockpit <subcmd> <id> <what to do>`, e.g.:

```
/cc cockpit terminal bmfb look at the recent error logs           ← default prod (cockpit)
/cc cockpit browser mpcw take a screenshot of the current page    ← default prod (cockpit)
/cc cockpit codegraph impact searchIndex assess the impact          ← default prod (cockpit)
/cc dev terminal aqou check the errors                            ← dev signal #2 → use cockpit-dev
/cc cockpit-dev codegraph file packages/...                       ← dev signal #1 → use cockpit-dev
```

When you receive such input:
1. Treat `<id>` as the concrete bubble identifier and pass it to the subcommand
2. Run `cockpit <subcmd> <id>` (or `<subcmd> --help`) first to see supported actions
3. Pick the right action to fulfil the user's task

## When you don't know which id to use — list bubbles first

If the user refers to a bubble semantically ("the alloydb proxy terminal" / "the admin page") rather than by id, list every bubble in the current project — each one carries any user-set title:

```bash
cockpit connection list --cwd $PWD
```

Output rows are TAB-separated: `<type>  <shortId>  <title>  <projectCwd>  <command-or-url>`. Match the user's reference against the title, take the `<shortId>`, then proceed with the typical usage pattern. Unnamed bubbles show `(none)` for title — fall back to the `<command>` column (terminal's command string / browser's URL) to disambiguate.

## Opening pages yourself

Do not ask the user to open a page by hand. `open` decides by what you give it:

- **A web page (http/https, localhost included) → a real Chrome tab** in the
  user's browser, in a "Cockpit" tab group, in the background unless `--show`.
  It has the user's logins, and a tab Cockpit opened is already allowed.
- **A local HTML app or file (md/json/csv/image/pdf…) → a console bubble** in
  the project that owns `--cwd` (default: your shell's cwd).

```bash
cockpit browser open http://localhost:3000     # → "wxyz  →  tab opened in Google Chrome"
cockpit browser wxyz snapshot                  # drive it
cockpit browser wxyz close                     # close the tab you opened

cockpit browser open ./report.html             # → "abcd  →  registered and ready" (bubble)
```

Tabs the user already has open are addressable too: `cockpit browser tabs`
lists every tab with its id (the user sees the same id in the OpenCockpit
Bridge toolbar popup). The first command on a tab the user has not allowed
brings it to the front and waits for them to approve it (per tab); if it times
out with "Waiting for the user to allow control", ask them to approve and
re-run — do not loop. When you are done with a tab the user allowed, run
`cockpit browser <id> release` to hand it back. `close` only closes tabs
Cockpit opened, never the user's own. While you act on a tab Chrome may show
"started debugging this browser"; that is expected.

Tabs can do what a person at the keyboard can, so do not hand these to the
user:

- **Dialogs** — an `alert` / `confirm` / `prompt` pauses the page. The command
  that opened it says so, and every other command fails at once with the
  dialog's text until you answer: `dialog accept [--text …]` / `dialog dismiss`.
- **Uploads** — `upload <ref> <file>…` on the file input (snapshot marks it
  `file`) or on the button that opens the file chooser; no OS dialog appears.
- **Inside iframes** — the snapshot includes them, cross-origin ones too; their
  refs look like `f7:e3#v1` and work with every command.
- **Drag** — `drag <ref> <to-ref|css>`, or `--dx/--dy` for sliders.
- **Whole page / one element** — `screenshot --full`, `screenshot <ref>`.
- **Test conditions** — `viewport iphone|android|ipad|<W>x<H>` (clicks become
  taps; add `--reload` when the site picks mobile markup from the User-Agent),
  `theme dark`, `emulate --network offline|slow-3g --cpu 4 --block "<pattern>"
  --media print`. These stay on, with Chrome's debugging bar, until
  `viewport reset` / `theme reset` / `emulate reset` — reset them when done.
  Chrome does not let extensions fake a timezone or locale.

In a background tab Chrome cannot deliver real input into a cross-origin
iframe or turn the wheel; those fall back to DOM events and the output says
so. Run `cockpit browser <id> show` first when real input matters there.

Any bubble id the user shows you works directly, even if that bubble is asleep
or its badge is grey: the command wakes and registers it (its project must be
open in a Cockpit window). Close bubbles you open — a registered bubble never
sleeps. For a bubble, `open` exits **2** when no Cockpit UI picked it up: no
browser window has this project open — check `--cwd`, and ask the user to open
it. It is NOT a reason to retry.

Two things to know about bubbles: they only work for projects that are open in
a Cockpit window, and **previewing a local `.html` runs it with full shell
access** — treat `cockpit browser open ./some.html` as executing that file.

## Getting detailed usage

Every subcommand's `--help` is the canonical reference — **it includes usage, flags, output format, exit codes, and examples.** Read it first:

```bash
cockpit --help
cockpit <subcommand> --help
cockpit codegraph <subsubcmd> --help
```

Unnamed bubbles show `(none)` for title — fall back to the `<command>` column (terminal's command string / browser's URL) to disambiguate.

## Opening pages yourself

Do not ask the user to open a page by hand. `open` decides by what you give it:

- **A web page (http/https, localhost included) → a real Chrome tab** in the
  user's browser, in a "Cockpit" tab group, in the background unless `--show`.
  It has the user's logins, and a tab Cockpit opened is already allowed.
- **A local HTML app or file (md/json/csv/image/pdf…) → a console bubble** in
  the project that owns `--cwd` (default: your shell's cwd).

```bash
cockpit browser open http://localhost:3000     # → "wxyz  →  tab opened in Google Chrome"
cockpit browser wxyz snapshot                  # drive it
cockpit browser wxyz close                     # close the tab you opened

cockpit browser open ./report.html             # → "abcd  →  registered and ready" (bubble)
```

Tabs the user already has open are addressable too: `cockpit browser tabs`
lists every tab with its id (the user sees the same id in the OpenCockpit
Bridge toolbar popup). The first command on a tab the user has not allowed
brings it to the front and waits for them to approve it (per tab); if it times
out with "Waiting for the user to allow control", ask them to approve and

"started debugging this browser"; that is expected.

  refs look like `f7:e3#v1` and work with every command.

- **Whole page / one element** — `screenshot --full`, `screenshot <ref>`.

  taps; add `--reload` when the site picks mobile markup from the User-Agent),

  `viewport reset` / `theme reset` / `emulate reset` — reset them when done.

iframe or turn the wheel; those fall back to DOM events and the output says
so. Run `cockpit browser <id> show` first when real input matters there.

open in a Cockpit window). Close bubbles you open — a registered bubble never
sleeps. For a bubble, `open` exits **2** when no Cockpit UI picked it up: no

it. It is NOT a reason to retry.

## Getting detailed usage

Every subcommand's `--help` is the canonical reference — **it includes usage, flags, output format, exit codes, and examples.** Read it first:

```bash
cockpit --help
cockpit <subcommand> --help
cockpit codegraph <subsubcmd> --help
```

---
name: cg
description: "Trace code and assess change impact via the pre-built symbol, call-graph and co-edit index."
---

Enter project graph exploration mode (CodeGraph).

CodeGraph = pre-built symbol + call-graph index + git co-edit view. Nine endpoints, each answers one class of question:

| Question | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| Where is X defined / which files share the name? | search?q=X |
| Export every function/method, optionally within a directory? | symbols?path=src&excludeTests=true |
| Who calls X? | callers?qname=X |
| What does X call? | callees?qname=X |
| Changing X affects which symbols? | impact?qname=X&depth=2 |
| What symbols does file F contain? | file?path=F |
| Which files are commonly edited alongside F? (conventional coupling / parallel registries) | coedit?filePath=F |

All responses are coordinates / file paths — never source bodies. (One exception: `search&includeLiterals=true` echoes each matched literal's own text in `value`.) More precise than grep's textual match, cheaper in tokens than Reading whole files.

## The 7 graph endpoints ({{BASE_URL}})

```bash
# search: find symbols by name → hits carry the same node shape as every other
#   endpoint, so a hit's startLine/endLine feed Read directly.
# q is normalized for naming style: user_profile / userProfile / user-profile / USER_PROFILE are equivalent
# limit defaults to 50 per category and is capped at 500; use symbols for a full export.
# All eligible candidates are scanned. Ranking: raw exact name > normalized exact
# > normalized prefix > normalized substring; ties use path, qualifiedName, then line.
# path limits the directory (including descendants); excludeTests=true filters every category.
# Tests are included by default. Small limits still find exact definitions after many fuzzy matches.
# Pass includeLiterals=true to also search identifier-shaped string literals (tool names, event names,
# config keys, route paths — the "looks like a name but isn't an identifier" strings). The response
# then carries an extra literals[] array with value / filePath / line / enclosingSymbol per hit.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/search?cwd=$PWD&q=<NAME>"
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/search?cwd=$PWD&q=<NAME>&includeLiterals=true"
curl -fsSG "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/search" --data-urlencode "cwd=$PWD" \
  --data-urlencode 'q=<NAME>' --data-urlencode 'path=apps/api/src/features' \
  --data-urlencode 'excludeTests=true' --data-urlencode 'limit=5'

# Full export: defaults to function + method, including indexed nested symbols.
# path is a project-relative directory including descendants. Omit it for the whole project.
# kind accepts a comma-separated list or all (real symbols only).
# includeSynthetic=true also includes unknown UI blocks (__imports__, __code_*).
# Repeat exclude for POSIX globs rooted at cwd. Quote globs; dot paths require explicit dots.
# Start broad exploration with a summary; no result-count cap or export cache.
curl -fsSG "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/symbols" --data-urlencode "cwd=$PWD" \
  --data-urlencode 'path=packages/feature' --data-urlencode 'excludeTests=true' \
  --data-urlencode 'kind=all' --data-urlencode 'format=summary'

# Save full exports to disk, then print only a bounded selection of candidates.
curl -fsSG "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/symbols" --data-urlencode "cwd=$PWD" \
  --data-urlencode 'path=src' --data-urlencode 'excludeTests=true' \
  --data-urlencode 'exclude=**/generated/**' --data-urlencode 'exclude=**/*.spec.ts' \
  -o /tmp/cg-symbols.json

# callers / callees: 1-hop call relations
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/callers?cwd=$PWD&qname=<QNAME>"
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/callees?cwd=$PWD&qname=<QNAME>"

# impact: transitive callers BFS (depth 1-5, default 2; out-of-range is clamped
#   silently, not rejected). `truncated: true` = node ceiling hit, list is partial.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/impact?cwd=$PWD&qname=<QNAME>&depth=2"

# file: file symbol tree (no source). Hierarchical: nested symbols live in
#   children[] — always an array, empty for leaves (never null / never absent).
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/file?cwd=$PWD&path=<REL_PATH>"

# coedit: files commonly edited alongside the target = git log history + current working-tree co-edits
#   catches "conventional coupling" the call-graph can't see (parallel registries / double-writes / sibling .md configs)
#   history[] entries may name PRE-RENAME paths (git --follow), so a path here need not exist today.
#   `cooccurrence` is a RAW COUNT; the ratio ships alongside as `probability`.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/coedit?cwd=$PWD&filePath=<REL_PATH>"
```

## Response shapes

Every endpoint speaks ONE node shape (call it NODE):

`{ filePath, qualifiedName, name, kind, startLine, endLine, declLine, params?[] }`

`startLine` / `endLine` span the whole symbol INCLUDING the doc comment glued above
a top-level declaration and any Python decorators, so `startLine` can sit several
lines above the `function` / `def` / `class` keyword. `declLine` is the declaration line itself (equal to `startLine`

`filePath:declLine`.

`params` is OPTIONAL: absent for non-callables (class / interface / type / enum /
const) and for languages without a tree-sitter grammar. `params: []` is different —
it means "0 parameters", not "unknown".

```

            files[]    = { type:'file',    label, hint?, target: { filePath } }
            symbols[]  = { type:'symbol',  label, hint?, target: NODE }
            literals[] = { type:'literal', value, filePath, line, enclosingSymbol? }
            # narrow on the outer `type`

            # excludedFiles[] = { filePath, reason:"source-too-large", sizeBytes, limitBytes }
            # exclusions cover the entire revision, before export filters
            # flat output; default kind=function,method; kind=all includes all real kinds
            # unknown display blocks require includeSynthetic=true
            # format=summary replaces symbols[] with files, byKind, byDirectory:
            # [{path, total, files, byKind}]; groups are immediate child directories
            # of path. Direct files use path or '.'. All export filters apply.
            # total is the count after filters; incomplete describes source-index coverage

            # children[] is always an array, empty for leaves (never null / absent)
callers   { qname, target: NODE|null, callers[]: { caller: NODE, callLines[] }, ambiguousIn? }
callees   { qname, target: NODE|null, callees[]: { callee: NODE, callLines[] }, ambiguousIn? }
impact    { qname, target: NODE|null, nodes[]: { symbol: NODE, depth }, truncated, ambiguousIn? }

            # probability = cooccurrence / totalCommits, precomputed. `cooccurrence`
            # alone is a RAW COUNT — never compare it against a ratio threshold.
related   { target, results[]: NODE + { score, relations[] }, coedit[], degraded, degradedReason?, ambiguousIn? }
affected  { testFiles[], byInput[]: { filePath, reachable, reachableTests[] },
            unresolved[], stats: { visited, bfsMs, truncated }, degraded }
```

## Related code and affected tests

Project graph endpoints share the base symbol/import/call index. Coedit reads Git on
request. There is no secondary analysis cache or warm-up phase.

Only Git working trees (including linked worktrees) are supported. Every
project-index query verifies Git membership and source content hashes, then
reuses unchanged parse facts and atomically publishes consistent relations.
Watcher events only record changes; they never trigger parsing by themselves.
Tracked `node_modules` files are excluded too. Tests remain indexed.
`symbols` and `search` with `excludeTests=true` filter test/spec/e2e names, test/tests/__tests__
directories, Python test_*.py/pyi and Go *_test.go; this recognition is heuristic.

Worktrees sharing a canonical Git common directory reuse identical per-path
parse facts and lookup maps. Relations are resolved independently, then equal
whole-file relation bundles share read-only storage. File membership, timestamps,
configuration, revisions and failures remain worktree-local. Published roots own
the shared storage; eviction releases their references, and the memory budget
counts each shared block once.

Known Git operations in progress or paused on conflicts reject ordinary
queries. Finish the operation first; an explicit UI rebuild can inspect the
current workspace. Large changes rebuild all relations at 500 changed paths,
or at least 20 paths representing 20% of the larger old/new source count.
Manual force rebuild reparses all admitted sources. Symbol-only file previews
stay local. Opening the function call graph queries the project index on demand
and waits for its relations (`file-functions&relations=1`). Source/file caps are reported as incomplete
coverage (`X-Code-Index-Incomplete: 1` on project queries). Sources exceeding
2 MiB (2,097,152 actual input bytes) are excluded; exactly 2 MiB is admitted.
The symbols response lists oversized paths, reasons and byte sizes in
`excludedFiles`, even when outside the export directory. Responses also
include `X-Code-Index-Revision`. Fingerprints do not make heuristic call
resolution exact.

```bash

# include=structural skips Git; include=coedit skips direct call relations.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/related?cwd=$PWD&qname=<QNAME>&topK=10&include=all"

# File-level reverse-import closure, with test-file recognition.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/affected?cwd=$PWD&files=<a.ts,b.ts>&depth=10"

# For large input lists, cwd belongs in the JSON body.
curl -fsS -X POST "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/affected" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"cwd":"'"$PWD"'","files":["a.ts","b.ts"],"depth":10}'

# Plain format emits test paths; diagnostics are returned in headers.
curl -fsS "{{BASE_URL}}/api/projectGraph/affected?cwd=$PWD&files=<a.ts>&format=plain"
```

`related.relations` contains `caller{callLines[]}`, `callee{callLines[]}`, or
`frequent-coedit{cooccurrence,totalCommits}`. Scores are ranking heuristics only:
0.4 per direct relation, plus 0.3 times the coedit probability. They are not risk
estimates. Coedit partners use their first real symbol as a navigation anchor;
the relation is evidence about the file, not evidence that this symbol changed.
The raw `coedit[]` includes non-code and historical paths and adds `totalCommits`
to each history row. Reuse it rather than calling `/coedit` again.

## Interpretation and limits

- Check `target !== null` before interpreting empty results. Unknown symbols
  return HTTP 200 with empty relations. Use `search` to locate the definition.
- Use `qualifiedName` verbatim (`Parent>Child`), and pass `filePath` to
  disambiguate. On ambiguity, `callers`, `callees`, `impact`, and `related`
  return HTTP 200 with target=null, empty relations and candidate paths in
  `ambiguousIn`. No target is auto-selected; no relations or coedit are computed.
  Retry with the intended filePath. The CLI exits 2 on ambiguity, including
  --json mode, while preserving the JSON response.
- For project/business overviews, query symbols with format=summary first,
  then narrow path/kind. Keep full exports on disk; never print every symbol
  into context. Read at most 30 selected coordinates per batch. Business
  ownership still requires module documentation and source confirmation.
- Static call resolution is incomplete. Exported singleton-instance methods,
  aliases such as `export const alias = original`, and dynamic dispatch can
  lack incoming edges. Empty callers or impact is not evidence of safety.
  Cross-check source/text search; `affected` offers a broader file-import view
  within the imports the index can resolve.
- `related.degradedReason` is `coedit-unavailable` when Git lookup fails, or
  `truncated` when the source index is capped. Empty successful Git history is
  a valid result. `degraded: false` does not establish complete call resolution.
- `affected` reports unresolved input paths and traversal truncation. Its test
  recognition is heuristic; returned tests do not prove behavioral coverage.
- Coedit history can contain pre-rename or non-code paths. These remain in
  `coedit[]` even when no indexed symbol is available to navigate to them.
- Read source using `startLine` / `endLine`; cite locations as `filePath:declLine`
  (`startLine` includes leading doc comments / decorators and will not match the declaration).
- `context` and `risk` have been removed. Use `search` + `related` to explore,
  and `impact` / `affected` / `coedit` to inspect change evidence.

Errors are `{ error, tag }`, including ValidationError (400), NotFoundError
(404), AppError (500), and InternalError (500).

  return HTTP 200 with empty relations. Use `search` to locate the definition.

  then narrow path/kind. Keep full exports on disk; never print every symbol
  into context. Read at most 30 selected coordinates per batch. Business

  aliases such as `export const alias = original`, and dynamic dispatch can

  recognition is heuristic; returned tests do not prove behavioral coverage.

  and `impact` / `affected` / `coedit` to inspect change evidence.

Errors are `{ error, tag }`, including ValidationError (400), NotFoundError
(404), AppError (500), and InternalError (500).

> Form: **text diagrams for the skeleton, pseudocode for the deterministic logic

Most review is static — read the snapshot, judge right/wrong; easy, never skip it. The hard

## 2. Reviewer

```python
def review(scope):
    static_surface  = all_changes(diff)

    # A judges as-written; B judges over-time. Same spot can be in both.

    findings = []

        findings += part_A(static_surface)       # checklist §2.A
        diagram = draw_solution_diagram(diff)    # §3 rules; working copy for the report
    if scope in ("all", "dynamic", "slice") and dynamic_surface:
        slices = enumerate_all_slices(dynamic_surface, ARCHETYPES)   # list ALL first
        for s in slices:                         # a missed slice = all its risks missed
            model = build_model(s)               # state diagram · timeline · trajectory
            for risk in RISKS:                   # §2.B, all six, every slice
                findings += evaluate(risk, model)
            coverage.add(s, "✗#n" if s has finding else "✓")
        # slice not modelled → coverage.add(s, "— not modelled: <reason>")

    for f in findings:
        f.consequence = "When <trigger>, <the promised behaviour> does not happen."
        f.origin      = revert_counterfactual(f)     # §3

        if not traced_to_birth(f) and f.kind == "race":
            f.probability += " needs dynamic verification: <what's missing>"   # keep the tier

    return ReviewerReport(findings, diagram, coverage)     # working notes stay with you
```

### 2.A Static checklist — triangulate against intent / input domain / surroundings

Only semantic problems tools can't judge (style / format / unused / type errors → linter).

- **A1 vs intent** — do name / signature / PR text / comments **promise** what the code
  does? Do error / boundary branches return the right thing, not the happy-path value?
  Comments and docs in sync?
- **A2 vs input domain** (#1 bug source) — null / empty / single / duplicate / boundary /
  overflow / negative / unicode / over-length? Error path as correct as happy path,
  including the error **shapes** that actually arrive (P3)? Resources closed, state
  consistent on early return? External input treated as untrusted?
- **A3 vs surroundings** — contract drift (all consumers updated?); **dependency
  contracts** checked in the dependency's source or docs (returns / throws / internal
  behaviour / defaults / units, P3); convention / layering; types bypassed by `any` / casts;
  security checks the siblings all have.
- **Wrap-up** — duplicated decisions; dead code; local perf (N+1, IO in loop, unbounded);
  tests: boundary / error assertions, red-before-fix, **test doubles behave like the real
  boundary** (P3).

### 2.B Dynamic checklist

`ARCHETYPES` — sweep all when enumerating slices:
- shared-state init + multi-write · state reused across processes / re-entry ·
  check-then-act across an async gap (TOCTOU) · fire-and-forget write + later read ·
  implicit context across a hop · **state machines inside a dependency** (auto-retry,
  backoff, cache, pool, buffer — what does the caller observe while it runs and once it ends?)

`build_model` — read who reads / writes (across features, callers, into dependencies), then
draw for yourself: **state diagram** (who changes it under what condition), **timeline**
(all actors on one axis, traced to where the state is truly born), **change trajectory**
(created / changed / read / overwritten / lost).

`RISKS` — evaluate every one on every slice:

| Risk | Look for |
|---|---|
| Order race | a writer before the initializer; "awaited here" ≠ first touch |
| Overlap / undercount | same event recorded twice, or by nobody |
| Lost update | stale read overwrites the correct value |
| Fail-open wrong value | degradation lets a wrong / missing value through; read the guard's actual comparison (`NaN` is false both ways) |
| Cross-process / re-entry | reused state cross-talks; implicit context lost over the hop |
| Provenance break | key value no-op'd / overwritten / wrapped / type-erased between source and use |

Uncertain about ordering or arithmetic → frame as satisfiability: free variables, only real
happens-before constraints, invariant; SAT = bug with its trigger, UNSAT = safe.
Disciplines: a census isn't done until order + overlap are verified · no downgrading on local
observation · green tests ≠ verification (was the bug's layer mocked away?).

## 3. Finding semantics

```python
def revert_counterfactual(f):
    if gone_if_reverted(f):          return "introduced"   # incl. half-landed changes: one side
                                                           # of a contract/enum/mirror updated,
                                                           # even if the line is outside the diff
    if harmless_if_reverted(f):      return "activated"    # this change made it reachable
    return "pre-existing"
    # never blank; unsure → likeliest + what would settle it. Orthogonal to severity.

def rate(f):
    if f.impact == "big" and (f.probability != "negligible" or f.irreversible):
        return "🔴"      # irreversible = data loss / wrong money / security
    if f.should_fix:  return "🟡"
    return "⚪"
    # a safeguard failing in the very scenario it exists for is rated by the harm it was
    # meant to prevent — "no worse than before the change" is not a downgrade
```

**"When <trigger>, <the promised behaviour> does not happen."** Mechanism → `Break`;
downstream → `Effect`. ("X instead of Y" smuggles in a downstream effect — state Y's failure.)

claim about behaviour (P3): every arrow is real control flow, arms that don't join in code
don't join here, every path drawn to where it ends. Lines never cross a box or each other — repeat a terminal box (e.g. the same fail-closed exit) at the end of each path rather than route a long line across the diagram.
Annotations in a right-hand column. Each finding marked **once**: `✗#n 🔴 <what>`.

REPORT = [                                  # exactly these four parts, nothing else
    "heading+verdict",   # "## Review: <target>" + "<N> findings (🔴a 🟡b ⚪c). Worst: <Consequence verbatim>"
    "diagram",           # §3; unmarked if no findings
    "findings",          # one block each, sorted
    "coverage",          # ```text block
]
# > 5 findings → index before the diagram, a Markdown list, one item per finding:
#   "- #1 🔴 introduced — <Consequence>"   (bare lines collapse into one paragraph)
# language = the user's; identifiers and file:line unchanged
# blank line before the "## Review" heading and before and after every code block
# test runs / scratch scripts / side notes → a finding's Why, or the last coverage line

def format_gate(report) -> list[str]:          # countable checks only; never judges content
    errors = []
    for f in report.findings:
        body = f.block.body
        if not body.is_fenced("text"):         errors.append(f"#{f.n}: body not in ```text")
        if body.line_count() > 8:              errors.append(f"#{f.n}: {body.line_count()} lines > 8")
        if body.max_line_width() > 100:        errors.append(f"#{f.n}: line > 100 chars")
        if body.has_sub_bullets():             errors.append(f"#{f.n}: sub-bullets")
        if f.block.heading != f"### #{f.n} {f.severity} {f.consequence}":
                                               errors.append(f"#{f.n}: heading ≠ Consequence")
    for line in report.coverage.slice_lines():
        if words(line.name) > 6:               errors.append(f"coverage: '{line.name}' > 6 words")
    if report.diagram.marks_per_finding() > 1: errors.append("a ✗#n marked more than once")
    if report.has_parts_outside(REPORT):       errors.append("content outside the four parts")
    return errors
```

Finding block — Markdown heading, body in a ` ```text ` block (plain text, no backticks,
continuation lines indented under the field):

````
### #1 🔴 When the provider redelivers the same webhook, the duplicate is not ignored

```text
introduced · every redelivery; depends on provider retry policy
Break:  ✗#1 dedup.ts:12 — the key includes the delivery timestamp,
        so a redelivery never matches
Effect: redelivery → processed again (handler.ts:58) → charged twice (billing.ts:90)
Why:    dedup must key on what stays stable across redeliveries;
        verified against the provider's retry docs
Fix:    key on the delivery id alone; add a test that redelivers the same payload
```
````

`Break` may carry a flat zoom-in of at most 3 lines when the mechanism needs it.

Coverage block — always present, one slice per line, marks `✗#n` / `✓` / `— not modelled:`:

```text
introduced 1 (🔴1) / activated 0 / pre-existing 0
S1 dedup lookup on redelivery     ✗#1
S2 concurrent first deliveries    ✓
S3 retry after handler crash      — not modelled: no retry path in diff
```

assert diagram arrows == real control flow; each ✗#n once, right-hand column       # P4
assert every slice ✓ / ✗#n / not-modelled; every finding has an Origin             # coverage
```

`build_model` — read who reads / writes (across features, callers, into dependencies), then

|---|---|

| Overlap / undercount | same event recorded twice, or by nobody |
| Lost update | stale read overwrites the correct value |
| Fail-open wrong value | degradation lets a wrong / missing value through; read the guard's actual comparison (`NaN` is false both ways) |

---
name: design
description: "Produce a code-grounded technical design and implementation plan when an approach, material tradeoff, or execution sequence needs separate review. Use for requested technical design, not implementation; straightforward changes do not need a separate design stage."
---

Technical design mode: establish how the work fits the existing system, why the proposed solution holds, and how to implement and verify it. No implementation.

Input: a SPEC, agreed requirements, a document path, or the agreement in the current conversation. QA and SPEC are useful inputs, not required skill dependencies. This is an optional reviewable artifact, not a mandatory stage before coding. When invoked for a straightforward change, give a brief approach and checks rather than manufacturing a larger design exercise.

## Workflow

1. Extract confirmed behavior, constraints, acceptance criteria, and prior decisions. Reference them rather than rewriting the specification. Separate requirements from earlier implementation suggestions; do not silently turn suggestions into constraints. When revising a design or designing around an existing implementation, reconcile each established constraint: retain it, explicitly supersede it with an authorized decision, or explain with evidence why it no longer applies. Compression or already-implemented behavior is not a reason to silently omit a constraint; preserve it explicitly or by a precise source reference.
2. Read applicable repository instructions and identify the concrete unknowns that could change the approach. Investigate only the relevant code, contracts, callers, or tests needed to resolve them; reuse sufficient evidence already available in the conversation. Cite material facts by file or symbol and distinguish inspected behavior, inference, and unverified assumptions. Stop when further exploration would not affect the design or the next implementation step.
3. Judge the proposed concepts and state model: consistent meanings, legal states, invariants, lifecycles, resource ownership, and side effects where relevant. Place rules with their owner, keep things that change together close, and let independently changing concerns remain separate. When sharing a mechanism, preserve each caller's distinct policy and lifecycle; similar code alone does not establish a shared responsibility.
4. Compare existing code, standard-library and platform capabilities, and installed dependencies before introducing a new mechanism. For a proposed abstraction, identify the actual duplication, isolation need, or direction of change it addresses; weigh that benefit against new concepts, indirection, state, dependencies, and migration cost. Prefer a simple function, data structure, or existing mechanism when sufficient. Pattern names, file length, caller counts, and diff size alone do not establish design quality.
5. Before recommending replacement or consolidation, explain which existing responsibilities remain necessary, who takes them over, and which boundary paths could invalidate the proposal. A defect in the old mechanism does not prove the replacement works. Investigate technical unknowns with scoped read-only checks where possible. If necessary guarantees lack evidence, keep the proposal conditional and put validation before dependent replacement or deletion steps. Plan the resulting structure as well as the new behavior: identify obsolete rules and representations to retire, and define the scope and exit conditions for any temporary coexistence. Keep cleanup within the task and its direct effects.
6. Emit the DESIGN using the structure below. Resolve technical choices using code evidence and repository conventions, stating consequential tradeoffs. Ask the user only when a choice needs their preference or commitment about goals, behavior, scope, compatibility, or cost; complexity alone is not a reason to ask. Make progress on independent parts and mark sections affected by open decisions provisional; do not reinterpret confirmed behavior to make a design easier.
7. Check the design against the requirements and actual code, then stop. Do not edit application code, install dependencies, run migrations, deploy, send messages, or start implementation agents. A design does not authorize execution of its steps.

## Output structure

Use the following section order for a stable, reviewable DESIGN, matching the SPEC style. Omit sections that add no useful information; merge short related sections under the first applicable heading while preserving the overall order. Match the user's language and repository document conventions.

```text
## Context          goal, source requirements, confirmed constraints and decisions;
                    reference the SPEC where available, do not repeat it
## Current          relevant responsibilities, data flow, contracts, and guarantees;
                    cite code, callers, and tests that establish them
## Approach         chosen design, ownership, boundaries, and end-to-end flow;
                    distinguish reused, changed, new, and retired behavior
## Alternatives     material alternatives and why the recommended design wins;
                    include the cost and limits, omit ceremonial comparisons
## Changes          affected modules and contracts, data/state transitions,
                    error and concurrency handling only where relevant
## Migration        compatibility, data migration, transition and cleanup,
                    rollout and recovery only when required by this change
## Implementation   ordered steps (S1…); each has an outcome, affected modules,
                    dependencies, and a completion check
## Verification     map acceptance criteria and preserved guarantees to checks;
                    identify existing coverage, needed tests and manual validation
## Risks            consequential assumptions, technical unknowns, evidence gaps,
                    and how and when to resolve them before dependent work
## Decisions        unresolved choices requiring the user, with recommendations
```

Scale the detail to the work; the section list is not a requirement to write ten chapters. A small change may need only Approach, Implementation, and Verification in a few paragraphs. Do not invent abstractions, interfaces, migrations, alternatives, or a file-by-file checklist to fill sections. For a new project, mark the existing-code baseline absent and ground the design in supplied constraints and verified platform contracts instead.

Write for skimming: each decision has one home; reference rule and acceptance IDs supplied by the SPEC. Include signatures, data shapes, diagrams, or pseudocode only when they resolve an implementation ambiguity. Steps must describe concrete outcomes and dependency order, not generic phases such as "implement backend" or line-by-line editing instructions. Leave low-risk local details to implementation; specify them now only when they affect feasibility, contracts, sequencing, or verification. Keep technical design and implementation steps together so their assumptions and verification remain connected.

## Decisions

Use the QA-style condensed decision record. Number questions so the user can reply with letters alone. Do not re-ask answered questions or add a generic approval gate. Technical uncertainty that can be investigated is not a user preference question.

**1. <question>**

```text
Drivers: <1–3 criteria>
A ★ <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>
B   <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>

★ A — <recommendation justified by the drivers>
```

Options must be mutually exclusive and cover the meaningful alternatives, at most three. End with “Reply 1A 2B, 'all as recommended', or correct anything above.” only when decisions remain.

## Follow-up and saving

On answers or corrections, emit only the delta:

```text
## Changed     <section/step>: <old> → <new>; answered decisions as
               <chose X over Y> — <to achieve …>, accepting <cost>
## New         newly exposed assumptions, dependencies, or decisions, if any
## Open        still-open decision records; none → state that none remain
```

Update dependent steps and verification when a design decision changes. Do not treat an answer as authorization to implement. When asked for a complete or final DESIGN, consolidate accepted changes into one self-contained document, removing resolved questions and obsolete alternatives.

Default to delivering in conversation. If the user requests a saved artifact, use their path or the repository's established technical-design location; ask for a destination only if neither is available. Updating the requested DESIGN is allowed; unrelated repository edits are not. Report the saved path. Do not create commits or branches unless requested.

Before delivering, check that:

- The approach covers the confirmed in-scope behavior and identifies where it belongs and how it will be checked; requirements were not silently changed or expanded.
- Earlier constraints and decisions remain traceable in the revised design, directly or by precise reference. Any replacement or retirement has a stated basis; implemented constraints still have a verification path rather than disappearing from the design.
- Material claims about existing code and contracts have evidence; proposed behavior and unverified assumptions are labeled.
- Concepts, legal states, lifecycles, and ownership are coherent where affected; shared mechanisms preserve callers' distinct semantics.
- New boundaries and abstractions address demonstrated needs with stated costs; any replaced mechanism's necessary guarantees have an evidenced successor, or the recommendation and dependent steps remain conditional.
- The planned final structure retires obsolete expressions; temporary coexistence has a scope and exit condition. Structural cleanup stays within the task and does not replace behavioral verification.
- Implementation order follows actual dependencies; unresolved prerequisites are visible before the steps that rely on them.
- Verification covers changed behavior and relevant preserved guarantees, with planned checks distinguished from checks actually run.
- The next implementation step is clear and supported by enough evidence. High-risk unknowns have an explicit validation point before dependent work; low-risk details may remain for implementation. Do not imply that all uncertainty is resolved or that a design proves the feature works.

skills.desc: Delegate a sub-task to a new Cockpit session in any project on any engine; returns at once, or waits for the result with --wait.
skills.body:
---
name: dl
description: "Delegate a sub-task to a new Cockpit session in any project on any engine; returns at once, or waits for the result with --wait."
argument-hint: "[--wait] <what to delegate, and optionally which engine / project>"
---

Hand a sub-task to a brand-new session that runs on its own — in another project directory and/or on another engine (codex, deepseek, kimi, glm, ollama, claude). By default you do NOT wait for it: you get a receipt back at once, and the child notifies the user when it finishes.

**`--wait`** — when the arguments contain `--wait`, wait for the child to finish and carry on with its result in this same turn. Strip `--wait` from the task itself. Only the flag decides this: without it, never wait, even when later steps look like they depend on the result — delegate, restate the receipt, and say the result can be checked later.

Use it when the work belongs in another directory, suits another engine, or simply should not block this conversation. For parallel work inside this same repository, your own subagents are usually the better tool.

## 1. Delegate

Decide: target `cwd` (absolute project directory), `engine`, a short `title`, and the task. Write the task as a self-contained brief — the child sees none of this conversation. Put anything longer than a line or two in a brief file, so no JSON escaping is involved:

```bash
BRIEF=$(mktemp /tmp/cockpit-brief.XXXXXX)
cat > "$BRIEF" <<'EOF_BRIEF'
<goal, context the child needs, constraints, what "done" looks like>
EOF_BRIEF

curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST "{{BASE_URL}}/api/sessions/delegate" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-cockpit-run-id: $COCKPIT_RUN_ID" \
  --data-binary @- <<EOF_JSON
{"cwd": "/abs/target/project", "engine": "codex", "title": "<short label>", "briefPath": "$BRIEF"}
EOF_JSON
```

- `engine` is inherited from the session you are running in when omitted — that is what the
  `x-cockpit-run-id` header above is for, so always send it. Spell `engine` out only when the
  task should run somewhere else, which for `/dl` it often should. Claude when the calling
  session's engine cannot be determined. `model` is optional and never inherited
- For a one-liner you may send `"prompt": "..."` instead of `briefPath` (escape `"` and `\`)
- Do not delete the brief file — the child reads it after you return
- A 400 names the problem (missing directory, unconfigured engine, too many delegated sessions running) — report it, do not retry blindly

The receipt: `{ cwd, engine, model?, sessionId, link, title, createdAt, parent? }`.

## 1b. Wait — only with `--wait`

The moment the POST has returned a receipt, open `{{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/dl/wait.md` and follow it before any status call. It holds the poll loop and the budget rule that keep the wait alive past your Bash timeout. Skip it and you will either block past the timeout and lose the result, or report an outcome the child never produced.

## 2. Reply — always restate the receipt

The receipt is the ONLY record of this delegation. Tool output is not searchable later, so repeat it in your reply text:

```markdown
Delegated **<title>** to <engine> in `<cwd>` — [open session](<link>)
```

Use the `link` exactly as returned.

With `--wait`, add the outcome right under it — the `status` and a summary of `lastReply` — then continue with the rest of the turn using that result.

## 3. When the user asks how it went

1. Find the receipt: first in this conversation; otherwise search past sessions with the `/ss` flow (query the title or topic — your earlier reply and the child session itself are both indexed)
2. Check it:

```bash
curl -sS --fail-with-body --get "{{BASE_URL}}/api/sessions/status" \
  --data-urlencode "cwd=<cwd>" --data-urlencode "sessionId=<sessionId>"
```

3. Report `status` — `running`, `done` (the last turn finished normally), `failed` (the engine recorded an error) or `incomplete` (stopped, interrupted or never finished; the user can open it and continue) — summarize `lastReply`, and give the `link`.
   `lastReply` is cut to 4000 characters; when `lastReplyTruncated` is true and you need all of it, repeat the call with `--data-urlencode "full=1"`.

Decide: target `cwd` (absolute project directory), `engine`, a short `title`, and the task. Write the task as a self-contained brief — the child sees none of this conversation. Put anything longer than a line or two in a brief file, so no JSON escaping is involved:

```bash
BRIEF=$(mktemp /tmp/cockpit-brief.XXXXXX)
cat > "$BRIEF" <<'EOF_BRIEF'
<goal, context the child needs, constraints, what "done" looks like>
EOF_BRIEF

curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST "{{BASE_URL}}/api/sessions/delegate" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-cockpit-run-id: $COCKPIT_RUN_ID" \
  --data-binary @- <<EOF_JSON
{"cwd": "/abs/target/project", "engine": "codex", "title": "<short label>", "briefPath": "$BRIEF"}
EOF_JSON
```

- `engine` is inherited from the session you are running in when omitted — that is what the
  `x-cockpit-run-id` header above is for, so always send it. Spell `engine` out only when the
  task should run somewhere else, which for `/dl` it often should. Claude when the calling
  session's engine cannot be determined. `model` is optional and never inherited
- For a one-liner you may send `"prompt": "..."` instead of `briefPath` (escape `"` and `\`)
- Do not delete the brief file — the child reads it after you return
- A 400 names the problem (missing directory, unconfigured engine, too many delegated sessions running) — report it, do not retry blindly

The receipt: `{ cwd, engine, model?, sessionId, link, title, createdAt, parent? }`.

## 1b. Wait — only with `--wait`

The moment the POST has returned a receipt, open `{{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/dl/wait.md` and follow it before any status call. It holds the poll loop and the budget rule that keep the wait alive past your Bash timeout. Skip it and you will either block past the timeout and lose the result, or report an outcome the child never produced.

## 2. Reply — always restate the receipt

The receipt is the ONLY record of this delegation. Tool output is not searchable later, so repeat it in your reply text:

```markdown
Delegated **<title>** to <engine> in `<cwd>` — [open session](<link>)
```

Use the `link` exactly as returned.

With `--wait`, add the outcome right under it — the `status` and a summary of `lastReply` — then continue with the rest of the turn using that result.

## 3. When the user asks how it went

1. Find the receipt: first in this conversation; otherwise search past sessions with the `/ss` flow (query the title or topic — your earlier reply and the child session itself are both indexed)
2. Check it:

```bash
curl -sS --fail-with-body --get "{{BASE_URL}}/api/sessions/status" \
  --data-urlencode "cwd=<cwd>" --data-urlencode "sessionId=<sessionId>"
```

3. Report `status` — `running`, `done` (the last turn finished normally), `failed` (the engine recorded an error) or `incomplete` (stopped, interrupted or never finished; the user can open it and continue) — summarize `lastReply`, and give the `link`.
   `lastReply` is cut to 4000 characters; when `lastReplyTruncated` is true and you need all of it, repeat the call with `--data-urlencode "full=1"`.

---

Implementation mode: build what was agreed, in small slices that each prove themselves, without stopping for sign-off.

```
input  = the path or brief given, else what this conversation agreed (a PRD, an analysis, a plan)
accept = its success criteria; if none can be inferred, ask once before starting
notes  = {{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/go/notes/<basename of cwd>-<feature>.md
                                                 # same task continued → append under a new round heading

while slices remain:
    pick the next smallest slice that runs and can be checked on its own
    implement it                                   # minimum change, KISS
    verify by running it: commands, requests, tests — not by reading the code
    if it fails: fix and re-verify, at most 3 tries
                 then mark it blocked, note why, continue with what does not depend on it
    for each choice the spec did not cover:
        cheap to undo  → take the simplest option, log it to notes
        costly to undo → stop and ask
    emit: Stage N — <what> — <how verified> — <result>

    ## End-to-end   the full user flow, run once: steps and result
    ## Decisions    the notes file as a markdown link: [<basename of cwd>-<feature>.md](<absolute path>)
    ## Residuals    what is left, blocked or known broken, with suggested priority
```

name: new-branch
description: "Cut a clean new branch off the latest origin/main and verify it matches the remote."
argument-hint: "[branch name; ask if omitted]"
---

# New Branch (create a branch off the latest mainline)

Branch off the latest `origin/main` so the starting point is clean and in sync with the remote.

## Trigger

The user asks to "create a new branch / new branch / cut a branch" and wants it based on the latest mainline.

## Scope (important)

This skill is **only responsible for quickly creating a clean new branch**, up to "verify right after cutting".

- **Do**: fetch → branch from `origin/main` → verify sync → output confirmation.
- **Do NOT**: explore / read code, spawn Explore / Plan agents, produce an implementation plan, or start writing code.

Any requirement description the user includes at trigger time (e.g. "improve the add-to-slack onboarding flow") is **only used to derive the branch name / record intent**, not a dev task to start here. Follow-up requirement refinement and implementation are discussed by the user in a new conversation and are out of scope for this skill.

## Pre-checks

1. Confirm the branch name (always in English, following the `<type>/<short-desc>` convention, e.g. `feat/credit-guard`, `fix/stream-recovery`):
   - User already gave a ready branch name → use it directly.
   - User gave a requirement sentence (e.g. "improve the add-to-slack onboarding flow") → **derive** an English branch name from it (e.g. `feat/slack-onboarding-flow`) and create it directly, no need to ask.
   - No derivable information at all → only then ask.
2. Confirm the working tree is clean (`git status`). If there are uncommitted changes, stop and ask the user how to handle them; do not force-switch.

## Steps

```bash
# 1. Fetch the latest remote mainline
git fetch origin main

# 2. Create and switch to the new branch off the latest origin/main
git checkout -b <branch-name> origin/main

# 3. Verify: should be 0 ahead, 0 behind
git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD
```

`git checkout -b <name> origin/main` in one step guarantees the new branch's start = the latest remote mainline; no need to update local main first.

## Verification

- `git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD` outputs `0	0` (0 ahead, 0 behind).
- `git status` shows you are on the new branch with a clean working tree.

Output confirmation: branch name, current HEAD commit, and sync status against origin/main.

## When to stop and ask

- No ready branch name and no derivable requirement description → ask.
- Uncommitted changes in the working tree → ask how to handle (stash / commit / discard); never discard on your own.
- A branch with the same name already exists → ask whether to overwrite or rename.

## Key principles

- **Start from the latest**: always base on `origin/main`, never on a possibly stale local main.
- **Never lose changes**: confirm before any operation that could lose the user's work.
- **Verify right after cutting**: use rev-list to confirm actual sync; never assume.

Give evidence-based advice when asked to take a look; implement within the agreed scope when asked to apply or fix.
skills.body:
---
name: pair
description: "A contextual programming partner for exploring code, designing solutions, writing code and technical documentation, planning work, reviewing changes, verifying behavior, and explaining decisions. Give evidence-based advice when asked to take a look; implement within the agreed scope when asked to apply or fix."
---

# Pair — Programming Partner

Work with the user on the current programming question, making informed engineering choices and implementing them reliably. Seek correct behavior, coherent responsibilities and code that is understandable and practical to change. Scale the work to the question; do not turn every invocation into a full audit or display a mandatory process.

## Resolve the current task

Use the current instruction and relevant conversation to determine the target, intended outcome, constraints and authorized actions. Prefer an explicit target or a clear reference to the ongoing discussion. If neither is clear and changes exist, begin with a read-only look at the relevant diff. Editor state is a hint, not proof of the target. Ask briefly only when materially different interpretations remain after checking available context.

A standalone "pair, take a look" requests advice. An explicit instruction to implement, fix, clean up or apply an agreed recommendation requests execution: complete it within that scope without asking for routine confirmation. Resolve references such as "apply the second approach" from the conversation. Preserve explicit restrictions and any conditions attached to the recommendation. Investigate unresolved technical conditions before relying on them; clarify conflicts in goals or constraints rather than silently changing them.

An advice question during authorized work does not cancel that work or enlarge it. Answer the question, incorporate valid steering and continue the active task as appropriate. A new topic must not inherit unrelated goals or action authority.

## Read the relevant guide

Choose by the current question and decision, not a keyword, file extension or task length. Read the guide for substantive work in that area; add another only when its detail is needed. A simple self-contained answer may need none. These are working guides, not separate agents or required phases. Users do not need to choose a mode.

| Current need | Read |
|---|---|
| Find an implementation, understand a module or trace relevant code relationships | [Exploration]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/exploration.md) |
| Clarify desired behavior, acceptance, constraints or the sequence of work | [Planning]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/planning.md) |
| Choose models, state, responsibilities, interfaces, dependencies or design patterns | [Design]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/design.md) |
| Write code, discuss how to express an implementation, or assess code taking shape | [Coding]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/coding.md) |
| Assess changed code, another review's findings, or simplify affected code when authorized | [Review]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/review.md) |
| Assess a concrete security concern or conduct a requested security review | [Security review]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/security-review.md) |
| Establish whether a claim, feature or fix holds and what the evidence supports | [Verification]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/verification.md) |
| Write or maintain technical documentation for users, developers or operators | [Documentation]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/documentation.md) |
| Explain code or decisions, or help the user learn through meaningful collaboration | [Learning]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/learning.md) |
| Recover, summarize or hand off the current task without losing its constraints | [Context]({{COCKPIT_DIR}}/skills/pair/context.md) |

For a bug, use exploration for the affected path, verification for reproduction and observations, and design if the repair needs a modelling or responsibility decision. Use coding for implementation and planning when sequencing the work matters. Follow the actual uncertainty rather than a fixed sequence or mandatory planning ceremony.

For implementation involving persistence, asynchronous work, cancellation, retries or concurrency, use both Coding and Verification to establish state and ownership contracts and challenge their failure paths. Investigation and verification follow the affected behavior, not the changed-file list. Scale their depth to the semantic impact and uncertainty, not patch size.

Cockpit resolves the links above beside this skill. When explicitly reading an unexpanded source copy or a standalone installation, resolve these same filenames relative to the directory containing this `SKILL.md`; do not guess paths from the project working directory. If a needed guide is missing, report the specific gap and limit the affected conclusion rather than inventing its contents. Use only available and permitted tools. Guide selection does not authorize delegation, infrastructure setup or external actions.

## Common judgement and execution rules

- **Understand actual behavior.** Read existing code before suggesting changes. Trace relevant callers, data flow, lifecycle and ownership far enough to assess the question. Distinguish observed behavior from assumptions and intended behavior.
- **Define scope by the outcome.** Distinguish the desired result, required constraints, negotiable objectives and assumptions. Ground necessary guarantees in the accepted outcome, relevant contracts or demonstrated consequences; do not promote a preferred implementation or hypothetical improvement into a requirement. Include changes needed to meet those conditions and keep independent improvements separate. Investigation does not expand authorization. Make consequential conflicts explicit rather than silently relaxing constraints or expanding scope.
- **Use appropriate structure.** Give rules meaningful owners. Keep concerns that change together coherent and independently changing responsibilities separate. Similar representation or code does not prove shared meaning. Existing conventions are evidence to assess, not guarantees of correctness.
- **Compare viable approaches.** Check existing implementations, platform capabilities and installed dependencies for semantic fit. Compare benefits, simplicity, cost and maintainability within the accepted constraints. Reassess the approach when evidence or cost changes its value to the goal. Neither the smallest diff nor a named pattern is the highest goal; avoid speculative mechanisms and respect explicit resource limits.
- **Carry the contract through the work.** Retain the accepted outcome, necessary guarantees and unresolved conditions across exploration, design, implementation and verification. When the approach changes, reassess the affected guarantees and their owners. An accepted design is not evidence of completed behavior, and a completed step is not necessarily the completed task. Existing conversation or project notes can carry this context; no prescribed artifact is required.
- **Keep edits relevant.** Preserve user changes and exclude unrelated cleanup. Prefer existing files when suitable; create files with a real responsibility. skills.desc: Clarify a requirement as a lean PRD: problem, goal, success, scope, assumptions, and only the decisions that need you.
skills.body:
---
name: qa
description: "Clarify a requirement as a lean PRD: problem, goal, success, scope, assumptions, and only the decisions that need you."
argument-hint: "[requirement]"
---

Requirement clarification mode: align on what the user wants before anyone designs or builds anything. No solution, no code.

```
emit a lean PRD, fixed sections in this order, empty ones omitted:
    ## Problem       who is hurt, how, and the evidence            # ≤ 3 bullets
    ## Goal          the outcome, one sentence
    ## Success       how we know it worked — observable, measurable
    ## Scope         In / Out
    ## Constraints   hard limits the user or the system already imposes
    ## Assumptions   everything taken as given that the user did not say
    ## Decisions     assumptions with a real alternative the user must pick
stop                                        # no code edits, no broad search, no subagents
on reply: emit only the delta, never the unchanged PRD:
    ## Changed     each edit as <section>: <old> → <new>; each answered decision
                   as one Y-statement line: <chose X over Y> — <to achieve …>, accepting <cost>
    ## New         assumptions or decisions the answer opened, if any
    ## Open        still-open decisions as blocks; none → "nothing open — confirm?"
```

Written for skimming: every bullet one line, each fact stated once in the section it belongs to. Stay at the level of the requirement — what and why, never how. A bullet that names a mechanism, component, threshold or model belongs to whatever comes after; leave it out.

Assumptions are the point: an unstated default that turns out wrong is the most expensive gap there is, because nobody knew it was a choice. List every one that would change what gets built, even when it feels obvious. Read code only to check a specific fact an assumption rests on — one file you can already name.

**Decisions** — a condensed MADR record per open decision: the question as a bold title, then a fenced text block with the decision drivers, the options, and the recommendation last:

**1. <question>**

```
Drivers: <criterion> · <criterion>
A ★ <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>
B   <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>

★ A — <why, in terms of the drivers, one line>
```

- Options mutually exclusive and exhaustive, at most 3. Gain / cost stay one phrase each.
- Drivers: the 1-3 criteria this choice turns on. ★ is always given, never "up to you", and argued from them.
- End with: "Reply 1A 2B, 'all as recommended', or correct anything above."

Good round: the user can answer with letters alone. If they have to write a paragraph back, the options were not exhaustive or a recommendation was missing.

skills.name: skillify
skills.desc: Distil a proven workflow from this conversation into a reusable Skill file.
skills.body:
---
name: skillify
description: "Distil a proven workflow from this conversation into a reusable Skill file."
argument-hint: "[placement directory] [target to skillify]"
---

# Skillify

Abstract "the thing you just pulled off" into a reusable skill. This is an **analyze → extract → save** flow:

- **Step 1 is always analysis**: first decide whether the conversation / recent context holds knowledge worth distilling into a skill. If not, say so and stop — never force it.
- The placement directory and other args are **only needed at the final save step** — do NOT front-load a "where should it go?" question.

Applies when the user says: "abstract this into a skill", "write up what we just learned as a skill", "do this automatically next time", "skillify this", "capture this workflow".

Core goal: **turn a one-time success into a stable procedure, not copy a transient chat into a prompt.**

## Arguments (all optional; used only at save time)

- **Trailing text** (after `/skillify`) = the object / lead to skillify; if omitted, distil from recent context.
- **Placement directory `<skills-dir>`** = where the skill lands; the canonical source goes to `<skills-dir>/<slug>/SKILL.md`. **Only needed at the "save" step**; ask only if the user hasn't provided it — never ask before analysis.

## Step 1: Analyze — is there knowledge worth capturing (scan → gate)

Answer "**should this even be extracted**" first. Most candidates die here, not in the writing.

### 1a. Three-phase scan: don't miss invisible skills

Review what you just did, sweeping each phase once, asking one question per phase: **is there a "non-obvious action / judgement" here?**

| Phase | What to scan | Why it's easily missed |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | How did you locate / trigger / diagnose the real problem? Which signal did triage use? | No visible deliverable — most often missed |
| Decision | What justified the judgement call at the sticking point? Any reusable criterion? | Treated as "intuition", not realized it can be codified |
| Solution | Is the execution skeleton / tool-combo / verification reusable? | Visible — easiest to fixate on |

The scan is about **breadth, anti-omission**: people naturally notice only "solution" (it has deliverables), while "discovery / decision" — the diagnosing and judging moves — are high-value yet invisible.

> The three phases are only for **scanning candidates**, not chapters in SKILL.md. The body should be organized by **failure mode / investigation action**, not by these three categories.

### 1b. The real gate: don't over-extract

For each candidate, all four must pass:

- [ ] **Recurs**: will you hit this kind of scenario again? (One-off → a note is enough, no skill.)
- [ ] **Non-obvious**: is there an action / judgement you "wouldn't know without looking it up"? (Obvious things aren't worth codifying.)
- [ ] **Cost**: is the cost of getting it wrong / missing it high?
- [ ] **Stable**: is the procedure stable, not bound to this session's transient context / data?

Missing "non-obvious" or "recurs" → basically drop it.

**If nothing passes the gate → tell the user "not worth a skill this time", explain why, and stop.** Do not force a deliverable, and do not ask for a placement directory at this step.

### 1c. Merge or split: the boundary question

If discovery / decision / solution **all** surface candidates in one scenario, decide whether they go into **one closed-loop skill** or **split into a combination**:

- **Will any single phase be invoked alone?** Yes → split; always entered from the top → lean merge.
- **Is the value inside a phase or at the handoff?** At the handoff (upstream expected-state / contract must reach downstream for verification) → merge; each phase self-contained, handoff carries no info → splittable.
- **Would merging make one unit carry orthogonal failure modes?** Yes (e.g. static breadth vs dynamic-reasoning depth) → split.
- **Does this phase run first in other problems too?** Fan-out ≥2–3 → split into a reusable leaf.

**Third state (need both)**: when the loop must stay intact but a phase needs depth / reuse, use **orchestrator + leaf** — one closed-loop skill holds the contract and verification, delegating orthogonal phases to reusable sub-skills.

**Default to one closed-loop skill.** Split only on a real signal (a phase reused by a second scenario, or attention spread too thin for depth).

### 1d. Classify: decides how to write, not whether to extract

| Type | Example | Skill focus |
|---|---|---|
| Investigation | pull sources → build timeline → locate issue | evidence sources, steps, output template |
| Debug | reproduce → red test → fix → verify | invariants, tests, acceptance |
| Tool-combo | chain multiple log/monitor/analysis tools | query order, correlation IDs |
| Habit/convention | directory structure, naming, placement | path rules, naming rules |
| Writing template | issue / PR / retro report | structure, tone, prohibitions |

**Do NOT** write one-off details into the skill (a transient session, a full specific chat, a temporary verification code, etc.).

## Step 2: Extract — distil stable principles and draft

> If 1c decided on a split or orchestrator + leaf, run Step 2 once for **each** skill to land (each its own directory).

### 2a. Distil stable principles

Break the experience into:

- **Trigger**: when this skill should be used
- **Input**: what the user might provide, what to ask when it's missing
- **Evidence sources / tools**: which sources, files, CLIs, logs to check
- **Steps**: the stable, reusable execution order
- **Output**: what to hand the user, or what artifact to create
- **Boundaries**: what NOT to do, when to stop / ask
- **Verification**: how to confirm the skill worked

Write principles, not a play-by-play.

### 2b. Choose a slug

Slug: lowercase, alphanumeric + hyphen, short and clear, verb/task- or topic-oriented. Before drafting, `ls <skills-dir>/` to avoid collisions and match existing naming style (when the save dir is known).

### 2c. Draft SKILL.md

Use the generic-compatible frontmatter:

```yaml
---
name: <slug-or-display-name>
description: "One line: what the skill does and when to use it."
argument-hint: "<optional, describe args>"
alwaysAllow: ["Bash"]      # optional
requiredSources: []         # optional
---
```

Suggested body structure:

```markdown
# <Skill Name>

One-line goal.

## Trigger / When to use
## Preconditions
## Workflow / Steps
## Output format
## Boundaries & prohibitions
## Verification
## Examples
```

Writing style:

- Instructions must be executable, not vague.
- Don't write dead behaviors like "after reading, tell the user the rules are loaded".
- Action-type skills proceed by default; ask only when a key argument is missing.
- Keep concrete paths, APIs, command examples, but scrub one-off sensitive data.
- Match the existing style of the target skill library.

### 2d. Icon (optional)

- Prefer 3D / color / skeuomorphic style, consistent with existing visuals.
- Recommended source: Microsoft Fluent Emoji.
- Filename must be `icon.svg`/`icon.png`/`icon.jpg`/`icon.jpeg`, placed in the skill directory.
- No ad-hoc hand-drawn SVG stand-ins unless the user explicitly asks. If none fits, ask first — don't force one.

## Step 3: Save — land it in the given directory

**Only now do you need the placement directory `<skills-dir>`:**

- User gave a directory up front → use it directly.
- Not given → ask **now** where to put it; do not pick a directory on your own.

Conventions:

1. **One skill, one directory**: `<skills-dir>/<slug>/SKILL.md` (required) + optional `icon.svg` / `references/` / helper scripts.
2. **Never drop a SKILL.md directly in the `<skills-dir>` root**: even a single-file skill gets its own subdirectory.
3. **Keep helper data/scripts in the same directory** so the skill is self-contained.

```bash
mkdir -p <skills-dir>/<slug>
# write SKILL.md into that dir; include helper scripts/data if any
```

`<skills-dir>/` IS the canonical source — no need to symlink elsewhere.

## Verification

```bash
ls -la <skills-dir>/<slug>/
```

- [ ] `SKILL.md` exists, frontmatter valid, `name`/`description` non-empty
- [ ] Body non-empty with executable steps
- [ ] No hardcoded sensitive info (accounts, tokens, transient session ids)
- [ ] Slug doesn't collide with an existing one

## Output to the user

When done, briefly report: skill slug, source path (`<skills-dir>/<slug>/SKILL.md`), whether an icon was added, whether helper scripts/data are included. Don't paste the full SKILL.md unless asked.

## Key principles

- The user wants a **captured capability**, not a copied conversation.
- **Analysis first**: decide whether there's knowledge worth capturing; if not, stop — don't force it, and don't ask for a directory early.
- The canonical source always lives in `<skills-dir>/<slug>/`; even a single-file skill gets its own subdirectory.
- Distinguish fact / hypothesis / to-be-confirmed; don't hardcode a solution too early.

---
name: spec
description: "Turn agreed requirements or a QA brief into an implementation-ready specification: behavior, contracts, boundaries, acceptance, and only the decisions that need the user. Use when asked to write or refine a SPEC, not to implement it."
---

Specification mode: make agreed intent precise enough that development and testing do not have to invent product rules. Design only as far as the work needs. No implementation.

Input: a requirement, QA result, document path, or the agreement in the current conversation. QA is useful input, not a required skill dependency.

## Workflow

1. Extract confirmed requirements and decisions from the supplied sources and conversation. Keep current behavior, requested behavior, and proposed choices distinct; never present a recommendation as an agreement.
2. Read applicable repository instructions. Inspect only the existing contracts, flows, and code needed to verify specific integration assumptions. Prefer named files and targeted searches; stop exploring once the specification has enough evidence. Cite material facts by source or path; label anything unverified.
3. Resolve contradictions using explicit user corrections and confirmed decisions. If material sources still disagree, expose the conflict as a decision rather than silently choosing. Preserve earlier decisions unless new information actually invalidates them.
4. Emit the SPEC using the structure below. Make useful progress even with open decisions; mark affected sections provisional. Ask only for choices that change product behavior, scope, compatibility, cost, or an important tradeoff. Choose routine implementation details using repository conventions and record consequential assumptions.
5. Check completeness and consistency, then stop. Do not write application code, run migrations, deploy, send messages, or start implementation agents.

## Output structure

Use fixed sections in this order; omit empty sections. Match the user's language and the repository's document conventions.

```text
## Context          problem, goal, sources, verified current behavior; keep brief
## Scope            In / Out; affected actors, entry points, and surfaces
## Behavior         numbered rules (R1…); eligibility, ordering, states, transitions,
                    boundary conditions, and invariants relevant to this feature
## Interaction      entry → action → visible result; loading, empty, error, and
                    recovery states where relevant; reference supplied designs
## Contracts        affected interfaces and data; ownership, authorization,
                    validation, compatibility, and errors where relevant
## Design           proposed integration and responsibility boundaries; persistence,
                    concurrency, retries, and external dependencies only if needed
## Acceptance       scenarios (AC1…) linked to rules; precondition/action/expected
                    outcome, with verification method and external evidence needed
## Delivery         migration, configuration, rollout, and rollback requirements
                    only when this change needs them; distinguish release blockers
## Assumptions      unconfirmed defaults that materially affect what gets built
## Decisions        unresolved choices requiring the user, with recommendations
```

Scale to the work. A small UI change may need only Context, Scope, Interaction, and Acceptance. Do not manufacture APIs, data models, infrastructure, or deployment work to fill sections. When repository rules make a contract authoritative, reference it and specify the required changes rather than creating a competing source of truth.

Write for skimming: each rule has one home; use IDs to reference it elsewhere. Tables help compare states or outcomes. Include technical detail only when it closes an implementation gap or explains a tradeoff. Avoid line-by-line coding plans and speculative future extensibility.

## Decisions

Use the QA-style condensed decision record. Number questions so the user can reply with letters alone. Do not re-ask answered questions or add a generic approval gate.

**1. <question>**

```text
Drivers: <1–3 criteria>
A ★ <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>
B   <option>
    + <gain>
    - <cost>

★ A — <recommendation justified by the drivers>
```

Options must be mutually exclusive and cover the meaningful alternatives, at most three. End with “Reply 1A 2B, 'all as recommended', or correct anything above.” only when decisions remain.

## Follow-up and saving

On answers or corrections, emit only the delta:

```text
## Changed     <section/rule>: <old> → <new>; answered decisions as
               <chose X over Y> — <to achieve …>, accepting <cost>
## New         newly exposed assumptions or decisions, if any
## Open        still-open decision records; none → state that none remain
```

Do not treat an answer as authorization to implement. When asked for a complete or final SPEC, consolidate all accepted changes into one self-contained document, removing resolved questions and obsolete alternatives.

Default to delivering in conversation. If the user requests a saved artifact, use their path or the repository's established SPEC location; ask for a destination only if neither is available. Updating the requested SPEC is allowed; unrelated repository edits are not. Report the saved path. Do not create commits or branches unless requested.

## Verification

Before delivering, check that:

- Every confirmed in-scope requirement has an observable acceptance outcome; implementation suggestions are not reported as requirements.
- Relevant failure and boundary cases have explicit outcomes, especially conflicting actions, permission boundaries, time cutoffs, and external failures.
- Rules, interaction, contracts, design, and acceptance agree; no invented current behavior, template identifiers, credentials, or delivery guarantees.
- External configuration or real-device validation remains explicitly pending until evidenced; writing a SPEC does not prove a feature works.
- Material unknowns are visible, resolved decisions stay resolved, and no session-specific product details have leaked into this reusable workflow.

skills.name: ss
skills.desc: Find a past Cockpit session — any project, any engine, any date — from a one-line description, and link to it.
skills.body:
---
name: ss
description: "Find a past Cockpit session — any project, any engine, any date — from a one-line description, and link to it."
argument-hint: "<what the session was about>"
---

Find the past session the user is describing. The user rarely remembers the exact words, so do NOT search their sentence verbatim — expand it into keywords, search, read the snippets, and judge.

## 1. Expand the description into keywords

Write 3–8 short keywords that would literally appear in that conversation:

- The distinctive nouns of the topic (a file, API, error, product, library name)
- Both languages when the topic is technical: e.g. `快照` and `snapshot`, `跨站` and `CSRF`
- Synonyms and the words the assistant would have used in its reply
- Short is fine — 2-character Chinese words match. Avoid generic words (`问题`, `代码`, `fix`) that hit hundreds of sessions

## 2. Search

Each `q` is one keyword; repeat `q` for more (or join alternatives with `|`). Always URL-encode:

```bash
curl -fsS --get "{{BASE_URL}}/api/sessions/search" \
  --data-urlencode "q=<keyword 1>" \
  --data-urlencode "q=<keyword 2>" \
  --data-urlencode "q=<keyword 3>"
```

Optional filters:

- `--data-urlencode "cwd=/abs/project/dir"` — only that project (and its subdirectories)
- `--data-urlencode "since=2026-09-01"` — only sessions updated since (ISO date or epoch ms)
- `--data-urlencode "limit=20"` — default 10, max 30

Response: `results[]`, best first, each with `engine`, `cwd`, `title`, `updatedAt` (epoch ms), `matchedTerms`, `matchCount`, `snippets`, and `link` (null when the project directory is unknown). `corpus` reports indexing stats; the first call on a machine may take several seconds while the corpus is built.

## 3. Judge, refine if needed

- Read the snippets; ranking is keyword-based, the judgment is yours
- Too many plausible hits → add a distinctive keyword, or use `cwd` / `since` if the user hinted at a project or time
- No hits → try synonyms, the other language, or shorter keywords
- Stop after 3 rounds; say what you tried

## 4. Reply

Give 1–3 candidates, most likely first. For each: title, project (basename of `cwd`), engine, date, one line on why it matches, and the link exactly as returned, as a markdown link:

```markdown
1. **<title>** — <project> · <engine> · <YYYY-MM-DD>
   <why this is the one>
   [Open session](<link>)
```

If `link` is null, give the `cwd` and `sessionId` instead. Never invent or rewrite a link.
